chapter.name: The Age of Reorganisation
chapter.blurb: The breakup of the Maurya Empire, the Shungas, Satavahanas, Chedis, southern kingdoms, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas and their art.

scope_in.item: The Kushanas and the art of Gandhara and Mathura

concepts.name: The breakup of the Maurya Empire: an age of reorganisation
concepts.description: The end of the Mauryas, new competing kingdoms and how they gained control.
concepts.idea: After the Mauryas, many kingdoms competed and the map of India was reorganised.
concepts.rule: The last Maurya emperor was assassinated around 185 BCE by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga. The empire broke up and many earlier tributary kingdoms became independent. The weak northwest was exposed to invasions. Some scholars call the period the age of reorganisation. Kingdoms competed through matrimonial alliances or force, and border areas were important for safety. Dynasties from within the subcontinent included the Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas; outsiders included the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas.
concepts.example: A king might offer his daughter in marriage into a neighbouring royal family to cement an alliance.

Who assassinated the last Maurya emperor?
questions.a: Pushyamitra Shunga

questions.q: Which dynasty came from outside the subcontinent?
questions.a: the Kushanas

questions.q: The period after the Mauryas is known by some scholars as the age of
questions.a: reorganisation

questions.q: Why did many new kingdoms appear after the Mauryas?
questions.a: Earlier tributary kingdoms became independent

questions.a: matrimonial

questions.a: The region became weak after the empire broke up
o: The region became weak after the empire broke up

questions.q: Why were border areas important to a kingdom?
questions.a: Controlling them kept the kingdom safe from attacks
o: Controlling them kept the kingdom safe from attacks

questions.q: Give two ways in which new kingdoms competed for control.
questions.a: Peaceful methods such as matrimonial alliances and the use of force in warfare.

questions.q: A king gives his daughter in marriage to a neighbouring royal family. This is a
questions.a: matrimonial alliance

questions.q: Which are dynasties from within the subcontinent?
questions.a: Shungas, Chedis and Satavahanas

questions.q: The period runs from the 2nd century BCE to the 3rd century CE. About how many years is that?
questions.a: From 200 BCE to 300 CE is about 500 years (the 2nd century BCE starts in 200 BCE and the 3rd century CE ends in 300 CE).

questions.q: Why is 'reorganisation' a good name for this period?
questions.a: Existing regions were reorganised into new kingdoms that constantly competed, and the map of India changed.

questions.q: Which shows that the empire's control was lost?
questions.a: Former tributary kingdoms declared independence

questions.q: Explain why a weak northwest was a risk to the subcontinent.
questions.a: The northwest was the entry route for outsiders, so a weak region invited invasions such as those of the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas.

questions.q: Why did the chapter say many artefacts might belong to multiple kingdoms?
questions.a: The period had many kingdoms with different art
o: The period had many kingdoms with different art

questions.q: Compare the situation before and after 185 BCE.
questions.a: Before, most of the subcontinent was under one Maurya empire; after, it broke into many kingdoms competing for power.

questions.q: Explain how empires and the weakening of central control lead to reorganisation.
questions.a: When the emperor is weak or removed, tributaries stop paying tribute and become independent, and regions reorganise into new kingdoms.

questions.q: Is a big empire or many small kingdoms better for people? Give reasons.
questions.a: A reasoned answer such as an empire brings unity but relies on force, while many kingdoms may compete and fight.

questions.q: Draw a timeline from 200 BCE to 300 CE with the Maurya end and five dynasties marked.
questions.a: A timeline with 185 BCE for the Maurya end and bars for Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushanas, Shakas and Sangam kingdoms.

concepts.name: The Shungas
concepts.description: Pushyamitra Shunga, the ashvamedha yajna, revival of Vedic rituals, Patanjali and Bharhut art.
concepts.idea: The Shungas revived Vedic rituals and patronised literature and art such as the Bharhut Stupa.
concepts.rule: Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga dynasty in north and central India. He performed the ashvamedha yajna, in which a horse and soldiers wander freely and the lands it crosses unchallenged become part of the king's empire; a challenge leads to battle. His empire was smaller than the Maurya empire and was gone a century later. Vedic rituals revived while other schools flourished. Patanjali compiled the Yoga Sutras. The Shungas added carved railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life to the Bharhut Stupa in Madhya Pradesh.
concepts.example: The Bharhut railings carry carvings of Lakshmi, singers and dancers.

questions.q: The Shunga dynasty was founded by ____ Shunga.
questions.a: Pushyamitra

questions.q: The Vedic ritual with a wandering horse is the
questions.a: ashvamedha yajna

questions.q: The Yoga Sutras were compiled by
questions.a: Patanjali

questions.q: The Bharhut Stupa is in present-day
questions.a: Madhya Pradesh

questions.q: In the ashvamedha yajna, territory the horse crossed unchallenged
questions.a: became part of the king's empire
o: became part of the king's empire

questions.a: battle

questions.q: Compared with the Maurya empire, the Shunga empire was
questions.a: smaller

questions.q: Why is the Bharhut art important?
questions.a: It contains some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art
o: It contains some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art

questions.q: Explain how the ashvamedha yajna established a ruler's supremacy.
questions.a: A horse with soldiers was left to wander; land it crossed unchallenged was claimed, and any ruler who stopped it had to fight to decide supremacy.

questions.q: The Shungas added carved railings to which monument?
questions.a: the Bharhut Stupa

questions.q: Sanskrit was a preferred language for
questions.a: philosophical and literary works

questions.q: Give two ways the Shungas supported culture.
questions.a: They patronised literature, art and architecture, such as carved railings at Bharhut, and Sanskrit works like the Yoga Sutras appeared.

questions.q: Why did the Shunga empire not last long?
questions.a: It was smaller than the Maurya empire and disappeared about a century after Pushyamitra.

questions.q: The revival of Vedic rituals did not mean
questions.a: other schools of thought vanished

questions.q: Explain what the Shunga relations with the Greeks show.
questions.a: After some initial military campaigns, Pushyamitra kept friendly relations with the Greeks and kept the empire safe from invaders.

questions.q: Why might rulers perform the ashvamedha?
questions.a: To declare their position as the most powerful king
o: To declare their position as the most powerful king

questions.q: Compare Maurya and Shunga rule.
questions.a: The Mauryas ruled almost the whole subcontinent, while the Shungas ruled parts of north and central India and lasted a shorter time.

questions.q: Explain how the Bharhut Stupa shows continuity of culture.
questions.a: It was probably built under Ashoka and the Shungas added carved railings and Buddha's life stories, showing how later rulers built on earlier work.

questions.q: Was the ashvamedha a fair way to expand a kingdom? Give reasons.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, since it could avoid war if unchallenged but led to battle if stopped.

questions.q: Write a short news report on a ruler performing the ashvamedha yajna.
questions.a: A report describing the horse freed, soldiers following, rulers who challenge or accept, and the outcome.

concepts.name: The Satavahanas
concepts.description: The Deccan dynasty, trade and coins, women in the dynasty, patronage and decline.
concepts.idea: The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan and grew rich from maritime trade and patronage of many schools.
concepts.rule: The Satavahanas ruled large parts of the Deccan from the 2nd century BCE, mostly in present Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra, with capitals at Amaravati and Pratishthana (Paithan). Their coins with ships show maritime trade. Agriculture flourished in the Krishna-Godavari system. Trade reached the Roman Empire; they exported spices, textiles and sandalwood and imported glass and ointments. Princes took mothers' names, as Gautamiputra Satakarni did. They were followers of Vasudeva but granted tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. The empire fragmented in the 3rd century CE.
concepts.example: The Naneghat caves near a trade route were used to collect tolls.

questions.q: Satavahana princes were often named after their ____.

questions.q: A famous Satavahana capital was
questions.a: Pratishthana (Paithan)

questions.q: Satavahana coins often show
questions.a: ships

questions.q: Which river system made agriculture flourish?
questions.a: Krishna-Godavari

questions.q: Why do ships on coins matter?
questions.a: They suggest maritime trade was important
o: They suggest maritime trade was important

questions.q: The Naneghat caves near Pune were used to collect tolls and ____.
questions.a: taxes

questions.q: Satavahana traders exchanged goods with the
questions.a: Roman Empire

questions.q: Why did the Satavahana empire break up in the 3rd century CE?
questions.a: Weak central control and economic decline
o: Weak central control and economic decline

questions.q: Name two goods exported and two goods imported by the Satavahanas.
questions.a: Exports were spices, textiles and sandalwood; imports included glass and perfumed ointments.

questions.q: Gautamiputra Satakarni was named after

o: scholars and monks of various schools

questions.q: What do the Nashik and Naneghat inscriptions tell about royal women?
questions.a: They show that queens such as Gautami Balashri donated land, and a widow queen performed Vedic rituals including the ashvamedha and made many donations.

questions.q: Why are Naneghat inscriptions important for the history of numbers?
questions.a: They have Brahmi numerals that resemble modern shapes, showing that modern numerals ultimately originated in India.

questions.q: The Pitalkhora yaksha was made by a goldsmith. This shows that
questions.a: craftspeople could work in more than one material
o: craftspeople could work in more than one material

questions.q: Explain how the Satavahanas' prosperity supported culture.
questions.a: Trade brought tolls and taxes, and a relatively peaceful period allowed literature, art and cave temples such as Karla to develop.

questions.q: Why might princes be named after mothers?
questions.a: It signifies the importance of royal women
o: It signifies the importance of royal women
It was a law of Rome

questions.q: Compare Satavahana trade with Maurya trade.
questions.a: Both used coins and routes; the Satavahanas stressed maritime trade to Rome, as seen on ship coins.

questions.q: Explain how the Satavahanas showed religious tolerance.
questions.a: They followed Vasudeva yet gave tax-free land to Vedic scholars and Jaina and Buddhist monks and helped make cave temples, letting many schools flourish.

questions.q: Was the Satavahana empire a success? Justify.
questions.a: It lasted for centuries, had prosperous trade and culture, but ended through weak control and economic decline.

questions.q: Design a Satavahana coin with a ship and explain its symbols.
questions.a: A coin with a two-masted ship, wavy lines for water and an inscription in Brahmi naming the king, showing sea trade.

concepts.name: The Chedis and Kharavela of Kalinga
concepts.description: Kalinga under the Chedis, Kharavela, the Hathigumpha inscription and rock-cut caves.
concepts.idea: Kharavela of Kalinga recorded his deeds on the Hathigumpha inscription and respected all sects.
concepts.rule: After the Mauryas, Kalinga rose under the Chedi dynasty. Kharavela was a devoted follower of Jain teachings, sometimes called the monk-king, but respected all schools. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar were likely made for Jain monks and are examples of rock-cut architecture. The Hathigumpha inscription in Brahmi records his victories and welfare works year after year. He claims a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions and to be a respecter of every sect and repairer of every temple.
concepts.example: Kharavela claims to have defeated an alliance of south Indian kings, but the location is unknown.

questions.a: Chedi

questions.q: Kharavela was a follower of
questions.a: Jain teachings

questions.q: Kharavela's achievements are on the
questions.a: Hathigumpha inscription

questions.a: bhikshu-raja, the monk-king

questions.q: The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves are examples of
questions.a: rock-cut architecture

questions.a: He was a respecter of every sect
o: He was a respecter of every sect

questions.a: near Bhubaneswar

questions.a: His accomplishments year after year, including victorious military campaigns and works for people's welfare.

questions.a: rock-cut architecture

questions.q: Kharavela claimed to have formed a council of
questions.a: ascetics and sages from a hundred regions
o: ascetics and sages from a hundred regions

questions.a: A ruler takes pride in extending protection to all schools of thought, respecting every sect and repairing every temple.

questions.q: Why is it hard to trace Kharavela's battle with the south?
questions.a: He claims to have defeated an alliance of south Indian kings but the location is unknown and he did not seem to invade the south.

questions.q: How did artisans carve regular chambers two millennia ago?
questions.a: With skilled use of chisels and hammers
o: With skilled use of chisels and hammers

questions.q: Describe the Udayagiri caves and why they are notable.
questions.a: Near Bhubaneswar, likely for Jain monks, with intricate panels, statues and spacious rooms cut into rock, showing craftsmen's skill.

questions.q: Why does the chapter compare Kharavela with Ashoka?
questions.a: Both rulers protected all schools of thought
o: Both rulers protected all schools of thought

questions.q: Compare the Chedis of Kalinga with the Maurya rulers who fought at Kalinga.
questions.a: The Mauryas conquered Kalinga in a war, while after their decline Kalinga rose as a powerful state under the Chedi kings.

questions.q: Explain why inscriptions are valuable to historians using the Hathigumpha inscription.
questions.a: It gives a dated record of a ruler's deeds and values in his own words, which helps historians know political events and beliefs.

questions.q: Should a ruler follow one faith but respect others? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes, as Kharavela did, because it keeps peace and lets learning flourish; a reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Write your own short inscription recording three achievements of a ruler.
questions.a: An inscription listing three deeds such as a victory, a well and repair of a temple, written in a formal style.

concepts.name: Kingdoms of the south: Sangam Age, Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas
concepts.description: Sangam literature, the Silappadikaram, and the three southern kingdoms with their trade and achievements.
concepts.idea: The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas flourished in the Sangam Age with rich literature and trade.
concepts.rule: Between the 2nd or 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE three powerful southern kingdoms, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, flourished. The word sangam means association, here an assembly of poets, and Sangam literature is the oldest in south India. The Cholas (capital Uraiyur/Puhar) included Karikala, who built the Kallanai or Grand Anicut, still in use, making the Kaveri delta the rice bowl of the south. The Cheras (capital Vanji) traded spices, timber, ivory and pearls with Rome. The Pandyas (capital Madurai) were known for pearls and naval power. The Silappadikaram tells of Kannagi.
concepts.example: The Kallanai diverts water from the Kaveri and is still in use.

questions.q: How did the Kallanai benefit people?
questions.a: It diverts Kaveri water to the delta, bringing more land under cultivation and giving irrigation to millions in Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Explain how the three southern kingdoms showed both rivalry and cooperation in culture.
questions.a: They often competed for control of the South, yet all patronised poets, traded overseas and contributed to culture and trade.

questions.q: Why do historians use Sangam literature?
questions.a: It shows the society and culture of the times
o: It shows the society and culture of the times
It is about trade laws only

questions.q: Compare the Cheras and the Pandyas.
questions.a: The Cheras ruled western Tamil Nadu and Kerala with capital at Vanji and exported spices and timber, while the Pandyas ruled from Madurai, known for pearls and naval power.

questions.q: Explain how trade connected the southern kingdoms to the world.
questions.a: Spices, timber, ivory and pearls were exported to Rome and West Asia, and Pandya pearls reached Kharavela, so coins and ports linked them abroad.

questions.q: Why is the Kallanai a good example of lasting engineering?
questions.a: It was built by Karikala, restored many times and is still used to irrigate millions, showing durable design.

questions.q: Write a short poem in Sangam style about a farmer in the Kaveri delta.
questions.a: A short poem mentioning the river, rice fields and generosity, in the spirit of Sangam poetry.

concepts.name: The Indo-Greeks and the Shakas
concepts.description: How Alexander's satraps became Indo-Greeks, cultural blending, the Heliodorus pillar and the Shaka calendar.
concepts.idea: Indo-Greeks blended Greek and Indian culture, and the Shakas gave India its national calendar.
concepts.rule: Satraps left by Alexander became independent as the Indo-Greeks and took over the northwest after the Mauryas. They were influenced by local culture, blending Greek and Indian elements in governance, art and language. The Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha, named after an Indo-Greek ambassador, praises Vasudeva as the god of gods. Indo-Greek coins were of gold, silver, copper and nickel, some with Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi. The Shakas (Indo-Scythians) ruled from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE and developed the Shaka Samvat calendar, adopted as the Indian National Calendar in 1957.
concepts.example: Dates on official publications are given in the Gregorian and Shaka Samvat eras.

questions.a: They were influenced by local culture and wished to appeal to Indians
o: They were influenced by local culture and wished to appeal to Indians

questions.q: How did Indo-Greek culture blend Greek and Indian elements?
questions.a: They arrived as conquerors but adopted local culture, producing a blend in governance, art, language and daily life.

questions.q: An inscription by a Greek ambassador praising Vasudeva shows
questions.a: cultural assimilation

questions.q: Which materials were used for Indo-Greek coins?
questions.a: gold, silver, copper and nickel

questions.q: What three precepts does the Heliodorus pillar mention?
questions.a: Self-restraint, charity and consciousness, which when practised lead to heaven.

questions.q: Why did the Indo-Greek rule end?
questions.a: It ended with the invasions of the Indo-Scythians or Shakas.

questions.q: A government publication shows dates in two calendars. They are
questions.a: Gregorian and Shaka Samvat

questions.q: Explain how Indo-Greek coins tell us about both Greek and Indian culture.
questions.a: One side often shows a king and Greek deities, but some coins show Indian gods such as Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi, showing the two cultures met.

questions.q: Why did foreign rulers adopt Indian customs?
questions.a: They were influenced by the rich local culture
o: They were influenced by the rich local culture
They were forced by the Mauryas

questions.q: Compare the Indo-Greeks and the Shakas.
questions.a: The Indo-Greeks descended from Alexander's satraps and ruled the northwest first; the Shakas came later, ended their rule and developed the Shaka Samvat calendar.

questions.q: Explain what 'cultural assimilation' means with examples from this period.
questions.a: It means outsiders adopting local culture and blending it with theirs, as Indo-Greeks used Vasudeva on coins and Heliodorus praised Vasudeva.

questions.q: Is a national calendar of foreign origin still 'Indian'? Discuss.
questions.a: Yes, because it was developed in India during the Shaka period and adopted as the national calendar; a reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Design a two-sided Indo-Greek coin using a Greek deity and an Indian deity.
questions.a: A coin with a king and a Greek deity on one side and Vasudeva-Krishna or Lakshmi on the other, with a short legend.

concepts.name: The Kushanas and the art of Gandhara and Mathura
concepts.description: The Kushana empire and Kanishka, the Silk Route, the Gandhara and Mathura schools and cultural exchange.
concepts.idea: The Kushanas controlled the Silk Route and fostered the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
concepts.rule: The Kushanas came from Central Asia, probably in the 2nd century CE, and their empire stretched from Central Asia to northern India. Kanishka was probably the most powerful ruler; a headless statue bears the inscription 'great king, king of kings, son of God, Kanishka'. His coins show Buddha and Shiva with Nandi. They held large parts of the Silk Route. The Gandhara school used grey-black schist and blended Greco-Roman and Indian features. The Mathura school used red sandstone and showed Indian deities with fuller figures. The period also saw the composition of the Mahabharata and Ramayana.
concepts.example: Kanishka's coins show the Buddha with a Greek-script inscription.

questions.q: The most powerful Kushana ruler was probably ____.
questions.a: Kanishka

questions.q: The Kushanas originally came from
questions.a: Central Asia

questions.q: The Gandhara school used
questions.a: grey-black schist

questions.q: The Mathura school used
questions.a: red sandstone

questions.q: Why is the Silk Route important for the Kushanas?
questions.a: They controlled parts of it, so trade grew
o: They controlled parts of it, so trade grew

questions.q: The Gandhara style blended Greco-Roman elements with ____ features.
questions.a: Indian

questions.q: Why did Kanishka put Buddha and Shiva on coins?
questions.a: To show respect for many schools of thought
o: To show respect for many schools of thought

questions.q: Which best describes Mathura art?
questions.a: A distinctly Indian style with fuller figures and less Greek influence
o: A distinctly Indian style with fuller figures and less Greek influence

questions.q: State two features of the Gandhara school.
questions.a: It emerged in the western Punjab, blended Greco-Roman and Indian features, used grey-black schist and made fine Buddha images with realistic anatomy.

questions.q: A sculpture of a Buddha with flowing robes and realistic anatomy in grey schist belongs to
questions.a: Gandhara

questions.q: A red sandstone figure of Kubera with a moustache is likely from
questions.a: Mathura

questions.q: Distinguish Gandhara and Mathura art on two points.
questions.a: Gandhara used grey-black schist and showed Greco-Roman influence, while Mathura used red sandstone and a more Indian style.

questions.q: Why is the headless statue of Kanishka historically important?
questions.a: Its Brahmi inscription calls him great king, king of kings, son of God, and its clothing and weapon tell about the ruler.

questions.q: Which shows Kushana religious tolerance?

o: Buddha and Shiva on Kanishka's coins

questions.q: Explain how the Silk Route helped the Kushana empire and India.
questions.a: By controlling parts of it, the Kushanas gained trade income, and India was connected to other parts of Asia and the West.
s: Connection with Asia and the West

questions.q: What does the period's art show?
questions.a: Cultural exchange with a dominance of Indian themes
o: Cultural exchange with a dominance of Indian themes

questions.q: Compare Kanishka's two coins.
questions.a: On one coin the king holds a spear with Buddha on the other side, on the other the emperor appears with Shiva and the bull Nandi.

questions.q: Explain how art in this period reflects peaceful co-existence of ideas.
questions.a: Sculptures show many deities such as Surya, Shiva and Buddha, and styles like Gandhara and Mathura mix cultures, laying groundwork for temple architecture.

questions.q: Which school, Gandhara or Mathura, would you say is more Indian? Justify.
questions.a: Mathura is more Indian because it used red sandstone and Indian deities with less Greek influence.

questions.q: Draw a Silk Route map with four cities from the chapter.
